utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. Before I take the appearances, the Chamber apologises for any inconvenience caused to the parties and the accused for the delayed start. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Belinda Pidwell, and Crispian Smith on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Merinda Stewart appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, and 0Aleksandar Aleksic for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the next witness comes, I have a number of administrative matters which I would like to raise. Can I say that it appears from what I've just been told by the Defence that there's unlikely to be any cross-examination of the next witness by the Stanisic team and that Mr. Krgovic's estimate of three-hours is well over what he actually expects to take. So it's likely that this witness, given that Your Honours have given me one hour, is going to finish well short of 2.00. But, Your Honour, that led leads me on to various matters. Your Honours, we have now worked out with the remaining witnesses which Your Honours said we should call before the 17th -- before the -- the break on the 17th of December, that, in fact, with the witnesses we can call, we will be finishing the week of the -- the end of the week of the 3rd of December, I -- no 5th of -- no. Just let me get that right -- 6th. Your Honours, we will not be going beyond that week, so there will be a full week free. One of the reasons is there is a particular witness, ST-228, who would have come under the -- Your Honours' ruling that we should call all witnesses but Ewan Brown and if Your Honours grant leave, the other witnesses that we've applied to add, before the break. He is also testifying in the Karadzic case. Your Honours, this is a witness who's testified a great many times; he's an adjudicated fact witness; he's not in the best of health; and, therefore, we would wish to combine him so that he only has to come to the Tribunal once with the Karadzic case, so that he testifies first in Karadzic. There would then have to be a day's break at least while his transcript was considered by the Defence. But for various reasons, as Your Honours know, the Karadzic case has not been sitting and is not going to re-sit until, I think, mid-December, sometime. It can only be in January. So we'd ask Your Honours' leave to carry that one witness, who's an adjudicated fact witness, 228, into January. So that he can be combined with the Karadzic case. Your Honours, that, therefore, means there will be a full week where there'll be no evidence, it's possible, to call. At the moment Your Honours order is that we should restart with the evidence on the 10th of January with Mr. Brown or the other two witnesses, if you give leave. I understand that the Defence application - and I think, perhaps, they should make it today because we need to know where we're going - is that we should not sit at all that week. So perhaps if I could sit down for a moment - there are other matters - to see if that is actually the application.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is precisely the application. And I believe -- I think two weeks ago or three weeks ago we informed Ms. Featherstone that that is going to be our -- our request, the kind request to the Trial Chamber. Because if you remember, we have -- due to the Serbian calendar, there is -- there is a difference of our -- our Christmas and our new year. And last year it was kindly acknowledged by this Trial Chamber and in most of the cases it has been acknowledged that the 13th and the 14th are the days off due to religious reasons, or actually a new -- a Serbian new year. Now, the -- having said that, it -- it -- it appears that -- that if we start on the -- on the 10th, then we will have two days and then -- or three days and then a break for -- for two days. And if -- I don't -- I don't think that -- that it -- it makes much sense that -- that we do it like that. Just for the -- for the purposes of -- of resources, witnesses staying here for a longer period of time, and the like. So our -- our suggestion is that we start on the -- the week of the 17th, and it is our estimation at the moment that we will finish all the remaining witnesses in that week. That is ... that is our position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I say something for -- I see Your Honours considering the matter. First of all, I mean, this application has been made in other cases and not been granted. But can I put it this way: The -- the Prosecution will not object -- we can move the witnesses, provided we know; but provided, that time counts towards preparation for the Defence case. And indeed the week off that we're going to have at the end of -- in December. That's our -- we're very anxious that this case should proceed. And one of the suggestions I'm going make is that we should have a 65 ter Conference before we all break for Christmas to see exactly where we're going and how long is going to be allotted for the gap between the Prosecution and Defence case. If Your Honours, say, accede to this request made by the Defence, as I say, we won't object, but we say that the time should count towards preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, the Chamber will -- will not make a decision on this immediately. But could we have the Defence's response to what Ms. Korner has just indicated, that the apparent week in December and the applied-for week in January would count towards the preparation time the Defence has.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we strongly oppose that. At the outset of -- at the very beginning of this trial, at the -- at the Status Conference, and on other Status Conferences, I clearly stated that the Defence requests two months for the preparation of the Defence case undisturbed. Your Honours, we cannot -- we -- we are forced to -- to move the Witness Ewan Brown because we can't prepare for him due to amount of material that has been disclosed to us recently or in the meantime. Now, that -- that is the reason why Mr. Brown, as -- as an expert witness, is coming in January. And that was acknowledged by the Trial Chamber. Your Honours, we have a huge problem with the exhumations. I would -- I would need every minute of it -- of the time to deal with these issues. I cannot -- and -- and I -- I really cannot accept that we -- that we start the preparation of the Defence case. And -- and, Your Honours, we lack the time to prepare for -- for these two very big -- big issues. The exhumations I will explain -- I will explain when I'm ready for the submissions, probably next week, beginning of next week; and I will explain what is the situation there. And the situation is a very complicated one from the point of Defence. Therefore, we -- we also understand, Your Honours, that at the end of the Prosecutor's case there is going to be a bar table motion. Now, we cannot really start preparing the -- the Defence case seriously without the -- without the bar table motion and then we -- that we see what -- what -- what exhibits are admitted in the -- during the Prosecutor's case. I mean, it doesn't say -- it doesn't mean, of course, that we are not preparing for the Defence case. We are doing that since -- since April this year. But the -- the -- the real reparation can only start the moment when the Prosecutor's case finish. I'm sorry, I wasn't prepared to make the submission because it wasn't suggested in the -- in the list that Ms. Korner was -- was providing to us last night that this is going to be an issue. She never said that -- that they are going to ask that the time be counted in the preparation of Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, in terms of the decision which the Chamber has to make, we now know you generally oppose that part of what the -- it isn't really an application, but the Prosecution's view differs from yours. But there is something that you have added which intrigues me, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. JUGE HALL: Intrigue is probably the wrong word; confuses me is probably more accurate. The -- this matter of exhumations. I know that the substantial element of it is with the Trial Chamber and we are in fact working on it, but I had been under the impression from when this matter was last raised that there was a subsidiary aspect in respect of which the -- both sides were trying to reach some accommodation. But did I hear you to say that there are going to be further submissions on -- do I gather from that, that these discussions have proved fruitless and therefore there's going to be a second part to this exhumations business which the Chamber is going to have to consider?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. The first -- the first question was a legal question: Whether or not the Prosecutor is allowed to add additional 1.700 victims to the -- to the list which do not appear in the schedules of the indictment. That is the -- the question which is now in -- before the Trial Chamber. The second part is that at that point when -- or actually at the point where we were first disclosed the database, the exhumations database, the Defence requested all the underlying documents for -- for the victims in the schedules to the indictment. Now, we have been disclosed another set of materials, and we've been discussing the -- the contents of this disclosure. Now, unfortunately, it appears that the -- that this amount of material which was disclosed to us on our request does not contain any of the information that we are -- that we need or that we hoped we will get from the -- from the Office of the Prosecutor. Therefore -- and it appears also that the Office of the Prosecutor does not have the documents which we asked for. That is our understanding at the moment. So -- so that is -- that is going to -- that creates a problem, Your Honours. And -- and that is going to be my submission. I have to -- to make a submission to the Trial Chamber and explain in detail what is the -- what the Defence see as potentially a really big problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, so we have been alerted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, can I say that -- there was a meeting between Ms. Pidwell and Mr. Zecevic and Ms. Savic last Friday where it was all carefully explained. We do not understand what the problem is but no doubt we will hear when Mr. Zecevic makes his submission. But, Your Honour, can I go back to what he said. First, the bar table motion will be filed next Monday at the latest, we hope. It's being worked on at the moment, so it won't be at the end of the case. The second thing is this: All Defence teams have a large number of lawyers working on them. In Mr. Zecevic's case, there are three in court at the moment, a legal assistant outside court, and whoever else. The same applies, as can you see, from the Zupljanin case. And the idea is that you divide the work so that if one person is in court or dealing with the witnesses, others are dealing with other -- other lawyers are dealing with other matters relating to the case. Mr. Zecevic said he didn't -- he wasn't aware I was going to raise it. Item number 2 states whether you are asking for the week of the 10th of January to be vacated. Now, Your Honours, I cannot see how Mr. Zecevic can say he's been taken by surprise. All we're saying is that the week that's going to be free in December and the week that's going to be in January should be used by at least one of the lawyers towards preparation of the Defence case. This case, as Your Honours know, for various reasons has lasted a lot longer than anybody anticipated, and we really should be getting a move on. And those are the submissions we make on that. So, Your Honours, obviously we would need to know, really, just whether you're going to - regardless of whether you agree with our submission that it should be added to the Defence time - whether you are going to vacate the 10th of January so that we can make arrangements, particularly with Mr. Brown, who has the problems that he's a self-employed contractor these days. Your Honours, then, I've dealt with the witness called in January --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, I nodded, but I suppose I should say for the sake of the record: Of course. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I next move to witnesses relating to the Mladic notebooks. Your Honours have had submissions on whether or not witnesses should need to be called at all. The Defence request is that they are both called under the provisions of 92 ter. We all agree, it seems, that there's no point in the two witnesses repeating the evidence they've already given. I should tell Your Honours that one of the matters that Your Honours raised, namely, that public evidence had been given about the diaries, yesterday in the Stanisic/Simatovic case the evidence was made public. So that is now a fact. So, Your Honours, the reason we're asking is because if you want us to call particularly one of the witness before Christmas, which we can do, but we need to know that, please, this week, because it means someone will have to go and see the witness next week for him to be called in the last -- last week of -- that we've got witnesses. So if -- we'd be very grateful if we could have the ruling - oral ruling would be fine - this week. Your Honour, the next matter is how the 92 bis witnesses are to be dealt with that Your Honours have agreed. In most cases we've noticed that a summary is read into the record of their evidence. Would Your Honours be happy with that as a -- as a method of dealing with them? Perhaps you would like to consider that matter at some stage, given that we will have time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I should say, otherwise the general public has no idea what all these witnesses say, there's no public record if they just go in like that. There's got to be some kind of acknowledgment of what these witnesses are dealing with. Your Honours, as I said, we suggest that the 65 ter Conference, before we break for Christmas, may be a useful thing to hold as to -- as to what's going to happen. And particularly in the light of Mr. Zecevic's protestations about the time needed. And, finally, Your Honours, Witness 223, again, an adjudicated fact witness who is due to testify next week, when contacted by VWS said that he was unwell and is -- was going to provide a medical certificate. A videolink has already been organised for ST - let me just get the number - 244 next week. 223 actually lives in the same general area. And so it may be just simpler if we have both of them by videolink. And I -- I don't believe the Defence have ever objected to evidence by videolink. And so if that's possible, perhaps Your Honours could let us know then we can get in touch to make the arrangements. The videolink has been arranged for next week for 223.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We have been alerted to that, and we will revert to you as soon as possible, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Your Honours, that's finally -- can I ask just to go into private session, please, to deal with one matter which relates to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we don't know whether the Defence was alerted to this matter, the videolink in respect of the witness - was it 233? But if -- 223. But if you are in a position to have considered it, it would be useful for us to hear from you now; if not, in the course of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were not aware -- we just got the information about it, so perhaps at the first break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... so we go back into --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Your Honours, that's quite right. This is something that just arose this morning, and so I didn't have a chance to notify the Defence about that. Could we go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we'll I -- we can say this in open session, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, finally, you will have seen on our list that there was an extra document added which wasn't part of the 65 ter package which was one which was late disclosed to the Defence because we had to get the permission of the provider. It was -- actually, it arose in the Brdjanin case but with a different witness. However, Your Honour, I'm not making any application to add that document to our list or try and produce it as an exhibit in the light of the -- the fact, I understand it, the witness who's now coming hasn't seen the document before. So -- until I saw him yesterday, I wasn't aware of that. So I'm not making the application, although it's on our list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, unrelated to this, we expressed our views to Ms. Korner yesterday in terms that we oppose the use of this documents because they have not demonstrated any justifiable reasons for late disclosure and adding it to 65 ter list. This document was admitted into the Brdjanin evidence through another document [as interpreted], so it was well known that this document existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So could we have the witness escorted to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... are we going for the normal break at 10.25, or whatever it is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, bearing in mind that the accused would have been here, I intend to take the -- to stick to the usual times.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. I think I speak, or at least I try to speak, a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your testimony. You are about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out that the solemn declaration that you are about to make does expose you to the penalty of perjury should you give misleading or untruthful evidence to this Tribunal. Now, then, would you please be kind enough to read aloud the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. And, sir, could we begin by asking you to state your full name and your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm Charles George Alexander McLeod. I was born on the 27th of March, 1963, in London.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what is your profession today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I build schools.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what was your occupation in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was working for the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. I understood that this is far from being your first appearance before this Tribunal, so I don't have to explain you the proceedings in court. The only thing I could -- the only information I could provide you with is that the Prosecutor has asked for one hour. You are a so-called 92 ter witness that -- which means that you -- the transcript of your previous testimony will be taken into account in this -- in this case instead of an extensive examination-in-chief. The Stanisic Defence ask for 30 minutes for cross-examination, and the Zupljanin Defence for -- three hours. So that's all. And I give the floor to Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On that last note, I don't believe those are now the time estimates. Perhaps we could establish that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One hour for you, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, one hour for me, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thirty minutes for Stanisic. And not more than three hours for --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I don't believe -- yes, I don't think that's right anymore. I think I raised that with Your Honours. I don't think the Stanisic Defence intend to cross-examine, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Not at all, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic will go first, and we may not, in fact, have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic go first. Okay. Thank you. And Mr. Krgovic, what are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think that I would take three hours. Most probably maybe 40, 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McLeod, first of all, can I just deal a little bit more with your background. I think that in -- prior to July of -- or June of 1992 you were in the British Army.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And had you been in the British Army for some 12 years by then?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I had been in for ten years.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ten. And had you achieved the rank of captain?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you then, in July of 1992, did you join, as it was then, the European Community Monitoring Mission, ECMM?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you go to Bosnia in July/August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You testified in the Brdjanin case on the 21st and 24th of June, 2002; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, in fact, during the course of the weekend, you were asked to correct a type-written version of the notes that you had made.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review the testimony in the Brdjanin case?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if asked the same questions, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: They would.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now just so that we can briefly run through the events that you described in the Brdjanin case, I think at the end of August, you took part in meetings in the Autonomous Region of Krajina area with Serb officials in order to make arrangements for an inspection that was to be undertaken by a committee that had been set up by, as it was then, the CSCE, now OSCE, as a result of the London Conference.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Those meetings took place in Banja Luka and later in Gradiska and Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Well, the initial meetings were in Banja Luka. By the time we had the mission with us, then we went to Gradiska and to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And I think had you dealings, inter alia, with Predrag Radic, as you understood it, the mayor of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One meeting attended by Stojan Zupljanin. And we'll look at the notes of that in a moment.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And also in Prijedor Milomir Stakic, also as you understood it, the mayor of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you accompany the CSCE mission which had been -- which was being led by Sir John Thomson when it visited Manjaca, Trnopolje, and the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Later on, were you present in November 1992 when Manjaca camp was closed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's right that you kept your own notes about the meetings and the visits, and based on those notes you wrote reports for ECMM.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, additionally, you were able to provide the Trial Chamber with photographs that you personally took yourself.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And at the end of those notes, which we went through in the Brdjanin case, you, in fact, recorded your own feelings about what you had seen during this inspection, and also in a letter to your father.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for Your Honours' note, the feelings he recorded are at the end of the typed version of his notes, which is the document at tab 4, which has been given the provisional number of 3338B, and it's page 57 of those notes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please make a pause between question and answer for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... Oh, yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can I ask you then, please, to look just briefly at a couple of your reports; in particular the one dealing -- where you met Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That has been given the number -- in e-court it's 3606. It's tab 9 of the documents, the 92 ter documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's going to come up on the screen in front of you. In this version, as you can see, the name of the interpreter has been redacted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, as this is going to be under seal, it better not go out to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, if we look at it, the interpreter was one that had been brought along by Mr. Radic; is that right, Mr. McLeod?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this was headed -- it's -- the date of your report was the 23rd of August, but it dealt with a meeting on the 20th of August, Banja Luka recce. And we see in the first paragraph that the team had a meeting with Mr. Radic, the mayor; Mr. Zupljanin, the Banja Luka chief of police; and Colonel Vukelic, a representative of the 1st Krajina Corps. Mr. -- perhaps can we with have a look, page 2 in English. That's a great copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've got -- apparently if you do something -- if you press the button to the right hand -- no, not ring-tail. At the top. That's it. Thank you. And I think it's probably page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic says in -- speaks and, in the middle of the page, says: "Here we have opened all our PW camps." Does -- "PW," I take it, stands for prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Until your head of mission can give us reports on our prisoner of war reports of people in the Green Berets and Ustasha camps, we will not allow you total freedom here." Was this a theme, Mr. McLeod, that ran through it, that -- that -- the insistence that there had to be investigation of what the other side was doing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then can we go, please, because it was a long meeting, obviously, and a long report, to page 6 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm afraid I haven't the faintest idea where it appears in the translation, where Mr. Zupljanin speaks. Maybe the Defence can assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's page 6 as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page 6, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm not going to read through it again, Mr. McLeod. 18 years on, outside what you recorded there, are you able to assist any further with any impressions had you about Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If you can just cast your mind back slightly, what appeared to be the relationship between Radic, Zupljanin, and Vukelic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: So, Radic was clearly the civilian and he was deferring to the military and the police in terms of security matters. And it was clear that he was the main interlocutor that we had during the meetings. But security was not within his -- within his control.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we go to the last page, please, of this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There you record your impression -- in fact, on the previous page you started with Radic and then Zupljanin. And, again, is there anything further that you can add after this length of time to what you recorded there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That's that document. I'd like you to have a look at one of the other documents, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, page -- sorry. 3619, tab 21.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the follow-up, second visit you had in Banja Luka on the 24th of August. On this occasion, the meeting was with Mr. Radic, and - we can see in paragraph 1 - Mr. Bulic, representing the Banja Luka Police. Did you understand at all what Mr. Bulic's position in the police was? Was that ever explained?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: If it was, I can't remember what it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Going down to item 3 on that first page, conversations. To begin with it's only Radic and his interpreter. And you say that Mr. Radic made a strong opening attack. "Did you get permission from the Bosanska Krajina government to arrange this visit? If not, why not?" Did you know what he was referring to by "the Bosanska Krajina government"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, they had established a government, and what they were trying to do was to get us to recognise that government as an independent government and, therefore, state. And that was impossible at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then there's a reference at the bottom to the London talks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now can we go, please, to the seventh page in English, and I hope it's the same page in B/C/S. Mr. Radic again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You -- was it you, actually -- I mean, I know there were other people with you, but it -- was it you asking the questions? because we see in the middle of that page Mr. Radic was then asked if there had been many examples of attacks in Bosanska Krajina against Croats or Muslims. Was it you that asked that or someone else?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I suspect that was somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And I haven't asked you that now, but can you tell us, because I don't think you record in your report who else was there, who else was with you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That would have been another English monitor called Barney Mayhew.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then he'd in fact been in the ECMM since 1991?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So he was more familiar with the area than you were.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Radic says there were not individual acts but that the war: "... unfortunately, from all three sides there were incidents, ugly ones, but not in the Banja Luka opstina. And then he gives a description of the killings, and talks about the regular military forces who are under strict control of their commanders but also those who just put on the uniforms, procure somehow the arms, and they do not decide, differentiate, who to mistreat. We are arresting them by the military and police, because by international convention men wearing uniforms and carrying arms are treated as prisoner of war. In war it's easy to get both, but we will clean them out in Banja Luka and also in other cities." And then over the page you record your comment. You say: "This strikes me as a formula for not according prisoner of war status to any group of men whom it is more convenient to treat as criminals." Could you just explain to the Trial Chamber what exactly you meant by that comment.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: It struck me that what they were saying was that at this time in this place there were a lot of people who may or not may not have been regular soldiers but who might have been wearing uniform and might have been armed who were doing things out of control, and they were trying to round them up. But he appeared to me at that point to be describing a scenario whereby anybody wearing a uniform and carrying a gun could actually be defined as somebody who is not a regular soldier and therefore a criminal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. With what end in mind? That's what I think I'd like to establish.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I -- I -- the inference being that if somebody was criminal, they didn't have to be treated with the rights of the Geneva Conventions in terms how you look after prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you. That's all I want to ask you about that document. And then the final one of your -- the reports, please, to look at, before we turn to the OS -- CSCE report, is document 3619 -- oh, I've done that, sorry. Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 3614 at tab 17. I'm afraid they haven't been put together in a chronological order. And this is the mission to -- the part of the inspection in the Prijedor report on the 3rd of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You set out that this meeting -- was -- this is part of a mission from the 30th to 31st of August, and as you explain, you escorted the CSCE mission group to Banja Luka with the aim of visiting prison camps. You explain how you had a meeting in Gradiska. And then talk about the -- Prijedor. And you there met Dr. Stakic, the mayor, paragraph 2. And, in addition to that, Mr. Kovacevic, who was also there, and we can see his interventions at page 3. However, I just want to ask you about, please, because you dealt with this in your testimony, the conclusions that you came to, which is page 5. First of all, your general impressions: "The version of events that led to the opening of Trnopolje that we were given by the mayor was in stark contrast to that given by the people we spoke to in the camp." Now, the report was written on the 3rd of September. Did you go to the camp after you'd had the meeting with Stakic or before?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: We met Stakic and then we went to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. "Conclusion. The authorities insist that they are acting in the best interests of all the people in their area, that they have no desire to get rid of the Muslim population. However, this just does not match what they are actually doing. And against this background, it is very hard to draw conclusions based on what is said. "The conclusion to be drawn from what we have seen is that the Muslim population is not wanted and is being systemically kicked out by whatever method is available." Was that conclusion based just on your visit with the CSCE mission or altogether on your experience since you had joined in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That was the conclusion that I had reached by that point in terms of my experience of working in the theatre over the previous couple of months.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. That's all I want to ask you about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to move on to the actual report that was produced, which will be, apart from the photographs, the last topic I'm going to ask about. Perhaps that might be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. The -- having regard to what we know in terms of what counsel will spend with this witness, the Chamber would wish to take advantage of the breaks to do such work on the several matters raised as it could. So the two breaks that we take today will be of 30 minutes' duration.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I can just -- if I can just explain to Mr. McLeod that he will be finished today so that he knows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours invited us to give our position on Videolink ST-223. Well, we haven't received the medical information and all that, but accepting what Ms. Pidwell told us about the -- the -- the witness condition, overall condition, we accept that he be called by video -- he testifies over videolink. However, Your Honours, the problem might be the documents. Because according to the situation as it stands now, we're supposed to give the documents for the other witness that is on the videolink by Friday this week. And we will not be able to provide the documents to the Registry for this other witness, due to this late notice. So, therefore, we would request that we be given time until Monday next week to provide the -- the -- our documents for cross-examination to the Registry. And we believe that -- that -- there is a sufficient time, because if we file -- if we give the documents on Monday, then the Registry will be able to organise the travel on Tuesday, because the videolink is on Wednesday, so ... That is -- that is the situation. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I think that the Prosecution appreciates that the medical certificate is a condition precedent to the Chamber agreeing to this, otherwise, practical suggestion. But the -- Mr. Zecevic's time-frame, will -- as he says, that would work. Do you agree, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes. But we won't -- I'm told there's -- we won't be able to get the medical certificate this week. I mean, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is it forthcoming? As long as it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... as long as we get an undertaking that it's forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, there will be -- yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm helpfully assisted by Ms. Pidwell. The medical certificate won't say he can't travel; it will simply say he's sick. So from that point of view, that's what it's going to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, could we have the witness back to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, I now want to look with you at the actual full report that was done by CSCE as a result of this mission, which has already been exhibited as P1599.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is -- was -- is not a document that needs to be under seal -- or not shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, just so that we make it clear, Mr. McLeod, I don't think you had any hand in actual writing this report nor saw it when it was published?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: No, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, you've had a chance to go through it, and I want to deal with the parts that you are able to assist on, in that they certain seem to be based on what you and the other members of the mission that you were with saw. Can I start by looking at -- we'll skip the -- well, perhaps we look, first of all, at page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm afraid, Your Honours, I can't assist with B/C/S. Hopefully they're all about the same pages, but ... Oh, sorry, it's not page 3. That's not the one I want. It's -- sorry. It's either -- one, two, three, four - page 5. Sorry. Page 3 of the actual report. If we're know showing the right page in B/C/S, perhaps the Defence would be kind enough to let us know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I simply want to look, briefly, at method of work. First paragraph. And then we see: "The northern group, chaired by Sir John Thomson, was given the task of investigating locations in northern Bosnia, also from west to east, including Sarajevo." And that's the group that you were with. Is that right, Mr. McLeod?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you actually accompany them when they went to Sarajevo, or were you just for the northern part?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I didn't go to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then can we go, please, straight away to the ninth page in English. And can we look at the paragraph that begins: "Lack of respect for civilian population."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The mission determined that a complete range of individuals, both male and females, young and old, are now being held throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina in various places of detention. We met with prisoners as young as 17, or even less, and as old as 83. The crucial point is that thousands are being held against their will or under conditions which make their departure from the places of their confinement virtually impossible." Mr. McLeod, does that paragraph accord with your impressions from the places that you visited?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then there is the categorisation of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go to the next page in English, and I hope -- I think it's probably the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Category C: "... people who were taken prisoner because they lived or worked in the zone of combat ... not taking part in hostilities but were seen as enemies due to their ethnic origin. "Their civilian (non-combatant) status should have protected them from detention. This category was easily the largest. "Our experience suggests that a comparatively small percentage of prisoners are genuine POWs. The remainder should never have been imprisoned. We are not impressed by claims that they were incarcerated for their own safety or simply because they happened to be resident in a combat zone. It's impossible to escape the conclusion that most prisoners are innocent people who have been seized as hostages to promote ethnic cleansing. They are pawns in vicious games played by nationalist politicians. These innocent people should be released forthwith." That claim, Mr. McLeod, that they were being incarcerated for their own safety, was that one that you heard being made personally?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what conclusion did you come to? As it was -- as is stated in this report, or a different conclusion?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I think it was quite clear that people had been removed from their houses and put into the various camps, not for their own safety but as a -- part of the process of getting rid of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, then, please, to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "All authorities told us that the prisoners they held were legitimate prisoners of war. Serb authorities also insisted ... they had the right to hold individuals taken in the area of the conflict ..." And then it deals with what international legal experts said. "Moreover, in our discussions with hundreds of detainees in Serb, Muslim, and Croat places of detention, we found an appalling number of individuals who we believe are, in fact, civilians with little, if any, direct connection with the conflict." Now, first, did you actually yourself see any of the Muslim or Croat places of detention?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Not during this mission, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And it goes on to repeat that: "We are very disturbed by the assertions from the parties that many of the people they hold under these severe conditions are being held for their own protection. Serb authorities in Prijedor, for example, insisted that they were protecting the Muslims from Muslim extremists who were fighting a guerrilla campaign from the former partisan stronghold of the" -- Kozarac -- it says "Gorazde," but I think that should be Kozarac "... mountain." Again, was that something you heard them say in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, further down the page, the responsibility of leaders.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I be told whether we're on the right page in B/C/S? I think probably not. No. Is that the right page? That's right. Yep. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The responsibility of leaders. "Despite the existence of warlords, the bulk of the evidence points to the responsibility of acknowledged leaders. The Mission believes that, in general, leaders exercise effective control over their military and civilian structures. Contrary to what is usually accepted, the so-called uncontrolled elements are marginal. They exist, but their importance has been exaggerated by various leaders who find them a convenient explanation for numerous barbarities. The mission have seen camps, well organised, with military personnel or policemen doing what they were told to do." In one of the earlier reports, Mr. McLeod, we looked at, we dealt with your view of what was being said to you by Mr. Radic about how by classing people as criminals they were able to avoid the conventions which applied to prisoners of war. This paragraph here, does that, again, accord with your impression of what was happening?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I think in practice the conclusion that I had reached after what Mr. Radic had said the first time, without having seen the camps, was that they were trying to twist things in one direction. Having seen the camps, my conclusion would actually be the opposite. They were trying to twist things in the other direction and therefore saying that a whole bunch of people who had nothing to do with the military were prisoners and they were holding them all as prisoners of war. And ... again it -- what they were saying was actually not what we were seeing in reality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. From your dealings with all the various parts of -- of the structures, as it were - the civilian, military, and police - did you conclude that the leaders did, in fact, control what was happening?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, can we go, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, could you specify your answer a bit. On what basis do you reach this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we wanted to visit, then we had to have permission, and permission came from high up within the regional government. And you had to have a permission and a stamp or a fax, and so permissions were sent by fax. But this was something which -- and you can see the interchange that we had where they were trying to persuade us to acknowledge the fact that it was their government who was authorising us to be there. So they had -- they had a structure, they had a government, they were trying to gain international recognition for the government, and it was clear that the structures that sat below that were then able to take us to the camps and were in control of the camps. And if you have five and a half thousand men in two camps, which you're taken to see by those who are acting on behalf of the people you've given your authority and you can see an order trail which takes you back to those people as being those who are in charge, then I think it's fairly clear that you've got a structure which is in control and has the ability to detain five and a half thousand people at their will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, can we go to the next page, please. At the bottom we can see the open centre at Trnopolje. "We would like to call the chairman's attention to the Trnopolje so-called open centre in the Serb-conquered area around Prijedor. This dismal location no longer has barbed wire surrounding it, and Serb officials insisted that the inmates were free to come and go as they pleased. Our interviews with the persons within that facility produced a vastly different perspective. Most of the 2.000 or so Muslims were civilians driven from their homes in the region by the" [sic] "Serb forces. Their residences have been burned, bombed, or occupied by immigrant Serb families, leaving them no local place to go to, should they wish to do so. Numbers of detainees who have left the camp have never returned. And when night-falls, the level of personal security reportedly drops precipitously. We discussed this situation with controlling political authorities and, as a result, have developed a plan of action which is set out in part 2." Mr. McLeod, you went to Trnopolje; does this part of your report accord with your experience?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Treatment of prisoners by authorities. With very few exceptions, camp authorities have little sympathy for the detainees. We witnessed the results of beatings, wounds, fractures, and other injuries in camps controlled by the" [sic] "Serbian, Muslim, and Croatian authorities and have reason to believe that innocent prisoners on all sides have been executed. The prisoners interviewed are reluctant in most cases to provide specific detail concerning atrocities, but many provided hints. We conclude that some camp authorities have treated the detainees with relative fairness, given the current circumstances, whilst" [sic] "others have been clearly abusive, or at least have tolerated mistreatment of detainees." Now, on this occasion, for this mission, you told us you didn't go to the Muslim and Croatian camps, but from the camps that you visited, Manjaca and Trnopolje, did you yourself see signs of injury to any of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. I certainly went into the medical centre in Manjaca and saw a number of men in there who had various injuries. I don't know what caused them, and they weren't telling, but some of them were fairly horrific.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's the next point I want to ask you about. It's already contained in the reports which we haven't gone through today but a part of your testimony. Were the people that you spoke to reluctant to discuss what had happened to them, as is stated here?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. So I -- I speak German and I was able to try and -- and make opportunities to go and talk to some of the men away from the minders who were with us. And on each occasion that I started a conversation, somebody, a camp guard or a minder, would then come and join in fairly quickly to listen to what was going on. But in those brief snatches of conversation, it was quite clear that they were interested to see people from the international community; they wanted to know how long they would be there; they were very reluctant to talk about what was going on and the conditions; and they certainly didn't want to talk about their conditions as soon as somebody was listening to the conversation. And I had a couple of conversations in Manjaca and a couple of conversation in Trnopolje, and each followed the same basic theme. They were quite clear that they were not combatants. They were quite clear that they had been taken against their will and had no idea how long they were going to be kept there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, then, please, to the next page because there's a brief description of what was seen at Manjaca. Under the heading: "Health of Prisoners." "Whilst many civilians in BH are said to be short of nutritious food, there can be no doubt that a majority of prisoners are more seriously deprived. In Manjaca, most prisoners exhibit signs of very serious malnourishment, including" - how do you pronounce that one - "cachexia, hair loss ... and muscle wasting." And then it goes on to say they admit to a weight loss of between ten and 40 kilograms during the two months of detention there, and in other notorious centres such as the camp at Omarska which the prisoners believe is now closed. Again, was that something you witnessed personally, Mr. McLeod?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. While I'm -- I have no medical training, so I couldn't comment on the medical diagnoses. But certainly the guys that I saw with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then at the bottom of that page and onto the next page: "It is not too strong to say that the vast majority of prisoners are living in fear, and some in terror, of their lives. This is reflected in their behaviour. They react immediately to commands to stand, sit, proceed to the eating places, and in many instances walk like humbled or degraded persons, with stooped shoulders and their hands behind their back. This was particularly evident in Manjaca and Konjic. Previous mistreatment by authorities has undoubtedly broken the spirits of many prisoners. Mental scars are likely to persist for a long time to come." Obviously you're not qualified to deal with that. But when you were at Manjaca, did you see behaviour as is described in this report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then medical services. Again it deals with Manjaca in the middle: "The hospital ward at Manjaca is completely unacceptable, with the ill and injured accommodated on the floor of a small former stable, with only a single blanket each for their comfort." You told us you went in there. Is that what you saw?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. And then I think, the rest of the report, there's a further long description of what was seen in each camp, and I needn't trouble you with that. Yes, thank you, Mr. McLeod. That all I ask you about this report. Finally, can we just go through the photographs that you produced, which ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. The first photograph that I would like to have up is 3601, which is at tab 6. Slightly out of order, I know, but that's the way they've been bundled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just explain to the Trial Chamber, Mr. McLeod, what that photograph shows.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly. So on -- on the 23rd of July, 1992, I was working in Karlovac, which is a town in Croatia on the border with the unprotected area, and this photograph depicts the crossing point in a village called Turanj. And we had been told that on that day a number of people might be crossing out of northern Bosnia into Croatia, and so we went to the crossing point to observe. And this photograph, which was taken at some point during the morning, shows an ECMM monitor and our interpreter. And you can see in the background a car being driven by people who are leaving. And there was a constant stream of vehicles during the day. And then during the night there was a constant stream of people who were being bused up to the Serb side of the crossing point and then told to get out of the buses because the Serbs wouldn't let their buses drive over into Croatia. And UNHCR had some very large trucks which they then drove across and put people into the trucks and drove them into Karlovac. And this went on all night. And our estimate was that about 9.000, but very, very hard to tell, crossed over in that one day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, can we go, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just one small point of clarification. I take it that the three soldiers we see are UN peacekeepers or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... could we next have up, please, 3607.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what that depicts, please, Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly. So this and the -- the - well, I have a number; I don't know how many you'll see - a series of photographs I took through the windscreen of my vehicle as we were driving back, having been to Manjaca and Prijedor. So this is on the road from Prijedor back towards Banja Luka on the 31st of August. And this -- this is just typical of what the houses looked like. And what you can see there are houses that have been burnt. So the roofs have been burnt off. They're not -- this is not half-built construction; this is somebody's house that has been damaged to the point where it is difficult to go back again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we then look at the next in this series, at 3608.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that the same road?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. This -- this -- I think what we have now is a series of photographs that I took as we were driving along the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, same road; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That -- that's right. And, again, I'm not sure how clearly you can see it on the screen, but you can see the smoke damage above the windows and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... actually can we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- the roof is gone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we zoom in on it. Because I think you've got your originals in front of you. Yep. Yes. 3610.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is there any indication of who lived in these houses? I mean, were they Serb or were they Muslim or Croat communities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, this had been -- this had been an area in which the people whom we'd meant in Trnopolje and Manjaca had previous lived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] You say it's on the road Banja Luka-Prijedor -- you say it's on the road Banja Luka-Prijedor, Prijedor to Banja Luka. Are you able to give a rough indication of what the nearest village was? No.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Not at this stage. I could take out a map and guess. But it would be a guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... yes, again that's 3610 -- 3610. And I think the last in this sequence is 3611.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I mean, there, Mr. McLeod, we see an example of there's one house which has obviously been destroyed surrounded by two that haven't. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Umm, I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... or is that --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I -- I think what you can see there is the small house on the left looks as if it's still being occupied, and the two houses to the right have pretty clearly been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From any inquiries you made and any of the conversation you had, do you know why one house was left standing and two are destroyed or semi-destroyed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: In this particular instance, I have no idea. But what was quite typical was to find that houses belonging to the ethnic group in the area in which one was at any particular time would have people living in them and their neighbour's house would be blown up, if the neighbour happened to come from the wrong ethnic group. And that was a pattern which one saw as much in Croatia as one saw in Serb-controlled parts of northern Bosnia, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And just so the Court understands - I don't think I dealt with this with you because it's not relevant to this particular case - you weren't just in this area of Bosnia; you were in a number of other areas of the former Yugoslavia, is that right, throughout your period?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yep. And I think the final photograph I'd like to ask you about is, please, 3617, which is at divider 19.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. So what you can see there, and, again, it's less clear on the screen than it is in the originals that I have in front of me, but a group of men carrying their possessions in -- in plastic carrier bags, following an ICRC Land Cruiser. So the white -- you can probably just about make out on the screen the cover on the rear -- on the spare tire of the back of the Land Cruiser and its brake light. I took this photograph on the 1st of October, 1992, and these are men who had been taken under the control of the ICRC from Trnopolje and they're crossing over into Croatia. And, again, on this occasion, the buses which the Serbs had provided to take them from Trnopolje stopped on the Serb side of the line at Turanj, and then we simply walked, through no-man's land, down through the village to the Croatian side and then the ICRC had arranged buses on the other side. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. McLeod, that's all you're asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, subject to cross-examination, I ask that the whole package be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. My name is Dragan Krgovic. On behalf of the Stojan Zupljanin Defence, I'm going to ask you questions about your testimony given here today. Since my English is not as good as that of the other participants, I will speak Serbian, which will be simultaneously interpreted into English. I will make an effort to speak more slowly so you can understand me better and the interpreters can interpret more easily. Let me come back to a part of your answer, sir, which you provided to a question asked by the Prosecutor about the second meeting in Banja Luka when you spoke to Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit P841.2. That's tab 21 in the Prosecution binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honours, I'm told it's 2D -- no. 3619. Sorry, 65 ter. Forget the 2D. It's 3619, 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 7 on the screen in both the English and Serbian language versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Here in this report you speak about incidents happening among the members of other ethnicities. As far as I understood, Mr. Radic, here, speaks about murders, or incidents, committed by some persons in uniform. And as you say, they somehow come by weapons and they are not picky about the people who they mistreat. These persons actually are Serbs who are dressed in various uniforms and commit various crimes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I would need to go back to be able to see what we said before that to understand the context. I'm sorry, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at this comment of yours. Mr. Radic was then asked if there had been many examples of attacks in Bosanska Krajina against Croats or Muslims. It's on the same page. It is marked as a comment. Obviously there was a question by a member of your team about crimes committed by Serbs against Croats or Muslims. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the witness wants to be able to read the whole thing to put it in context before he answers Mr. Krgovic's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. So to answer the first part of the question, what he's talking about at the top of the page relates to what he's heard that is happening in Sarajevo, I believe. I'm not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Take a careful look at page 7, please. The first comment: [In English] "Mr. Radic was then asked if there had been many examples of attack" [as interpreted] "in Bosanska Krajina against Croats or Muslims?"

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Sorry, and then your second question related to the comment. And so, yes, that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here Mr. Radic was asked about crimes committed against Muslims and Croats or, in other words, he was asked about attacks committed in Bosanska Krajina. Correct? I saw you nod, but please say your answer, because otherwise it can't be recorded.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly. So, yes, at this point he is talking about what was going on in Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then he says that there were such incidents, ugly ones, from all three sides but not in the Banja Luka municipality. And then he continues to say that there were 13 killings and even killings among Serbs. Then two were Croats, one gypsy, and two others. And he continues to say: When it comes to regular military forces, they are under the strict control of their commanders, but there are also those who just put on uniforms, procure somehow weapons, and do not differentiate who to mistreat. This is basically the continuation of Radic's presentation, and he speaks about people who commit such crimes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That's what he's saying, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radic goes on to say: We are arresting them with the assistance of the military and the police, because under international conventions [as interpreted] men wearing uniforms and carrying arms are treated as prisoners of war. In war, it is easy to procure both uniforms and weapons, but we will cleanse Banja Luka and other cities of them. Here Mr. Radic speaks about these very people who are outside the chain of command, and he is saying what the Serbian authorities are doing about that; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. And I think if you then look at my comment on the next page where I say that "this strikes me as a formula for not according prisoner of war status to any group of men whom it is more convenient to treat as criminals," that in practice what he was describing was a scenario whereby you had Muslims who had got weapons and were wearing uniforms but who might not have been part of a military formation, as opposed to Serbs who were wearing uniforms and carrying weapons and were not under the control of the Serbian authorities. And clearly I can't remember the conversation as it took place, but the fact that I wrote the comment that I wrote at that time would suggest that I understood that he was talking about the -- the -- the Bosnian Muslim extremists as opposed to Serbs. But, in practice, I can't remember the conversation now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And basically what you put down here does not at all mention Muslims or Croats or members of other ethnicities. Mr. Radic, here, speaks about Serbs who commit certain crimes and he says that they are being arrested. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I -- I -- I can't remember, and so it would be foolish to try and draw a conclusion other than looking at what I wrote down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, based on what Mr. Radic said about how they treat uniformed Serbs who commit crimes, you drew a conclusion that the same could be applied to Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I -- I -- I wouldn't -- I wouldn't want to try and interpret it. What I think he was saying - and I think the reason why I wrote the comment that I wrote - is that I think he was setting out his stall in terms saying this is how we deal with people, and therefore he -- I -- what I -- what I guess I understood at the time, based on the report that I wrote, is that he was describing a scenario in which he had an excuse -- he. The authorities had an excuse for picking up Bosnians, Muslims, whom they wanted to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a careful look at this part where you noted Radic's words. You will agree with me when I say that there's no mention made of members of other ethnicities here. He is just saying that Muslims and Croats are being mistreated and harassed and about the treatment the Serb authorities afford to these people. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The translation is bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, here in this section you will agree with me that Mr. Radic speaks about the way the Serb authorities treat Serbs who commit certain crimes or harassment of Muslims and Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. He was asked if there's been examples of attacks against Croats or Muslims, and so in -- yes. In that context, he is then saying that there had been incidents on all three sides, but not in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you will agree with me when I say that no mention is made here of any actions taken against Muslims and Croats, but, on the contrary, he was promising you that he would cleanse Banja Luka and other towns where there are people who commit such crimes against Croats and Muslims and that these people will be arrested; isn't that correct? If you look at the last paragraph of Radic's words as related by you, that's basically the meaning, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. And -- and then, as I said earlier on, I also wrote a comment at the time, and because I wrote that comment, I'm assuming that actually I thought there was something else going on in what he was saying. But at 18 years' distance, we're stuck with the words that I've got written down in my report as opposed to my actual memory of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your impression was, when you were visiting Manjaca, that the Serb authorities -- or, rather, the military authorities you had an opportunity to speak to at Manjaca, that they considered that all persons detained at Manjaca were prisoners of war; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that, according to you, they strove to widen the circle of persons to be considered prisoners of war, even beyond the standards that you were familiar with; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: They described all the people that they were holding at Manjaca as prisoners of war. And my understanding of someone who is a prisoner of war is somebody who has been engaged in combat and is wearing a uniform and carrying a weapon, as opposed to someone who is a civilian who happens to be living in a combat zone. And the impression that I formed was that most, if not all, of the people that we saw were not wearing uniform and claimed not to have been combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you will agree with me when I say that at the time there was a dilemma that one had to face on the occasion of each exchange of prisoners in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that the war that went on there was -- were very from any organised combat with -- between uniformed armies that are controlled by the respective governments and honour the rules of war. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are you suggesting that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. One part of my question was badly interpreted. That there was a dilemma the representatives of the international community in Bosnia faced when making an honest assessment of the type of prisoners that you encountered, that the war waged there was far from any organised combat between uniformed armies serving recognised governments and honouring the rules of war. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: No. I -- I think it was quite clear, and not just in northern Bosnia but in -- in -- in each of the various areas where I worked, that there were political and military structures in place. And under those political and military structures, you had police, both military and civilian police, and it was quite clear that those structures were working on behalf of the direction provided by the politicians and interpreted by the military and political -- and police commanders.
