And so you could see regular army units and police units and so on which clearly had a structure and a hierarchy. And then you could also see, in each area, that there were civilians who were caught up in -- in the mess and -- and so you -- you could see Serbian civilians in Croatian-controlled areas, for example. As well as seeing Bosnian or Croatian civilians in Serbia-controlled areas who were clearly not combatants but who were being pushed around by those in uniform. So, I'm sorry, I disagree with your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And furthermore, you are aware that neither age nor gender were an obstacle to participating in the civil war that was being waged then in Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I don't see that age or gender is a -- is a barrier to taking part in warfare in various different places. However, I didn't see any evidence of very young people -- I can't remember seeing examples of women carrying weapons across any of the parties, particularly. No, so -- so -- by and large not, no. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you will agree with me when I say that there are, or that there were, various kinds of uniformed armed groups and individuals who participated in this conflict; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Quite clearly on -- on -- on -- actually, on all three -- on all three sides, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And some of these groups are the product of those who we can consider only local warlords; others are sort of civil protection; and others, again, are the armed wing of a right-wing political party. And then individuals were mobilized directly from their houses and fight in civilian clothes. Do you agree with this assessment of mine of the situation in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I probably agree with parts of it, and there are other parts were I can't really comment, because I'm not in a position to agree or disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P1599. Could we please go to page 8 of this document. It's page 8 in the Serbian version, and I believe that's it's the previous page to this in the English version. I apologise. It isn't this one. It should be page 7 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at the last paragraph, please. What I just put to you in the form of questions is the very content of the report shown to you by Ms. Korner, and you commented on these paragraphs with the Prosecutor. Please read these paragraphs carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with the assessment given in the last paragraph on page 8 in English?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. And -- and so what I said in my -- in my response to you was that there are bits of it where I'm quite clear, because of what I saw, that this is correct. And there are some bits where, because I didn't actually see it with my own eyes, I can't agree with it. I didn't see people who had been mobilized in civilian clothes carrying weapons, so I can appreciate that may have been going on, but I didn't see that. But I'm certainly aware that there were groups on all three sides who were acting not entirely within -- within the -- the normal command structure, although, again, I suspect that at some level all of them actually were under some degree of control. But ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But the crux of the matter is that these people whom you talked to when you visited these detention centres were in -- civilians. They could easily have been members of these armed formations, only they didn't have any fire-arms on them -- I apologise, they didn't wear any uniforms.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: They may have been. But then, again, they may not have been. And, I'm sorry, I don't know. But the impression that I had formed was that they had not been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is what you concluded on the basis of the answers that they gave to you, when you asked them about this?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. And some of them looked pretty old.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, of course, someone who had taken part in combat but is captured without uniform would deny having been involved in combat because they would like to gain freedom, and they would deny any participation whatsoever in any conflict. Is that right? Because the next question asked was when they were going to be set free.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure where the question is in that. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Are you -- I'm asking you: Is it normal to expect that the people who were captured and are keen to be set free to deny having been involved in any conflict or carrying arms or fighting in any other way?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Sure. I guess -- I guess that, in terms of the Geneva Conventions -- and this might be straying a little bit, but if you're not in a uniform, then the assumption might be that you're a spy and then you're treated quite differently, actually. Historically, that was certainly the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, of course, you are well aware that according to the Geneva Conventions the civilians are also afforded the status of POWs who are assisting armed forces and who have certain links with military units?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I'm not an expert on the Geneva Conventions, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, are you referring to the concept known as "levée en masse"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Precisely so. I was going to ask the witness if he is familiar with that concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You heard the comment made by Judge Harhoff. Are you familiar with this concept?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm more interested in whether Mr. Krgovic is familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am. I have prepared this, but the next document that I intend to show was the Geneva Conventions. However, since he said that was not an expert in the Geneva Conventions, I'm going to stop this whole line of questioning. But I do have a few more questions on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Time for the break, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we return in 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are Your Honours taking half an hour on this break as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not going to ask you any more questions about the Geneva Conventions, in light of the answers that you had given. I am interested in another subject that you discussed with the Prosecutor, which is the issue of Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look now at page 21 of the document that are already have on the screen. Let me just check whether the pages in both versions correspond. And that's in Annex C.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar that within the context of solving the problem of Trnopolje there were certain proposals made by the European Monitoring Mission and that it was decided -- or, rather, concluded, that the individuals held at Trnopolje be evacuated to various other locations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Right. So the English version doesn't match the B/C/S version. However, and I think that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your indulgence, please. That's page 23 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's still not the right page. We still don't have the right page, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... page 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: 25. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. So these were recommendations being made by the OSCE, or whatever it was in those days, as opposed to the ECMM. So these recommendations were made by the CSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the photograph shown to you by the Prosecutor where one can see the jeep of the ICRC and the process of evacuation of inmates from Trnopolje was actually implementation of this memorandum, and the organiser was the International Committee of the Red Cross. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I don't know if it followed this report. But chronologically it did. And, yes, the evacuation was organised by the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the last sentence of the first paragraph, which reads: "Whatever their longer term hopes, no one wishes in present circumstances to return to their homes in western Bosnia, because the local administration cannot or will not guarantee their physical security." In your responses to the Prosecutor's questions, was said that you heard from the Serbian sounds [as interpreted] that one of the reasons for those people being at Trnopolje was because it was impossible to guarantee their safety if they stayed at home. Does that collate or correspond to the impressions that you have after talking to the people at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. So the Serbs in Prijedor explained that the people in Trnopolje there were for their own protection. So they were there to be protected them from something, not quite clear what. And the people whom I spoke to in Trnopolje made it clear that it -- they couldn't go home because it was not safe to go home. I think that what the Serbs in Prijedor were telling us didn't really stack up, didn't make sense, because, in practice, I think the people, the Serbs in Prijedor, were the people who were causing -- who were creating the scenario, the situation, in which it was impossible for these people to go home. That was the impression that I formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As you just said, there was another reason for their feeling unsafe, which was possible attacks on those people by the Serbs if they returned home from these centres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In contact with the authorities of the republic -- or of the Krajina, did you discern that any measures had been taken for those people to be guaranteed or provided safety once they are released from the centres? I just wanted to add that I was referring to local authorities as well, in addition to the ones mentioned.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware that there were any -- I'm not sure I understood the question, I'm sorry. Just try one more time, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It was a lengthy question and part of it was not interpreted correctly. So, in your talks with the local people in Prijedor, or with the people from the Autonomous Region of Krajina or the Government of Republika Srpska, did you inquire whether it was possible for those people to be guaranteed safety if they are released from these detention centres where they were being kept?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Um ... I'm not sure we asked the question exactly the way that you're asking me. And so I -- I would have to go back to my -- my understanding of the fact that they were saying that the reason why people were in Trnopolje was for their own safety, and so, presumably, they felt that they could guarantee their safety if they were in Trnopolje but possibly not if they were elsewhere. I can't remember somebody asking exactly the -- the question exactly the way that you've framed it, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please go back to page 13 of this report, Chapter 2, entitled: "Recommendations."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 15 in the English. Can we please have page 16 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you look at sub-item (b), which reads: "No prisoner should be released into a dangerous situation. There must be adequate and supervised protection so that the prisoners may go to any place within BH of their choice ..." Now my question is: When you talked to Mayor Radic and you mentioned the prisoners at Manjaca, did he tell you that a number of people from Manjaca were released and that they were in Banja Luka at the moment and that the Muslim body called Mehamet [phoen] provided accommodation for them precisely because it was unsafe for those people to go back to their homes where they had originally been captured?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I can't remember. But if that's in the report, then I'm quite happy to go back to the report to look at it, if you'd like me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My next question is as follows: When you presented the assessment of the impossibility of their return and unsafety, you were not aware of the efforts that Republika Srpska was making at the time to ensure that these people enjoy personal safety and protection once they return to their homes?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I object to the form of that question. "You are not aware of the efforts that Republika Srpska was making at the time to ensure these people enjoy personal safety" presupposes that that's what the evidence is. Mr. Krgovic can put any document that he wants to, or ask the question in -- in a different form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was just a prelude to my next question, and, in that respect, I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit P607, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a letter from Stojan Zupljanin, whom you saw at the meeting. In this letter, he is writing to the local chiefs of police and giving them an instruction or direction that had been issued by the Ministry of the Interior and other bodies from the Serbian Republic with relation to the closure of these centres. And in paragraph 3, it says: [In English] "There is some information that indicate that isolated individuals might be attacked or threatened in some other way after their return to their home areas. Therefore, we call the attention of SJB chiefs and other officials to their obligation to take appropriate measures to protect these individuals, guard their houses and property, and prevent any attempt in threatening or in any other way intimidating these people." [Interpretation] And in the last paragraph: [In English] "In co-operation with municipal bodies of the Red Cross organisation, humanitarian organisation" [sic] "and other bodies, it is necessary to provide food, accommodation, medical, and other forms of help to the above-mentioned returnees." [Interpretation] Sir, you certainly didn't inquire with your collocutors whether anything had been undertaken in that sense, and I suppose that you had never seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you talked with the officials, you did not ask them whether any measures were undertaken to provide security for those people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I can't remember whether that question was asked exactly the way that you're asking it. For what it's worth, the impression that I had was that that was not what was going on. There was a flow of people from houses to places like Trnopolje and then out, as opposed to from Trnopolje back to houses, because the houses that they had come from were no longer habitable. So that -- that was the overriding impression that I formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you prepared your report and when you mentioned Kozarac and took those photographs, you did not inquire about the conflicts in Kozarac and whether the houses had been damaged during war operations. You did not ask for information from the other side, i.e., from the Serbs, but, rather, based your report on your conversations with the Muslims. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Um ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... which report? I'm sorry, Your Honours, it's not clear. Which report is Mr. Krgovic referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the three reports entered into evidence that pertain to his visit to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In those reports, when you drafted them, you did not ask the Serbian side about the conflicts in Kozarac or about how the houses were damaged; instead, you based -- your report only on your talks with the people at Manjaca and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I think it's fairly clear - I hope it's fairly clear - that the first two reports are my visits to Banja Luka and then the reports that I wrote about the visits to Manjaca and Trnopolje. But in the two first visits, I was trying to give a flavour, not a complete verbatim transcript like this one, but a flavour for what it was that the people we were meeting, the Serbs that we were meeting, in Banja Luka were telling us; and so I was reflecting, as accurately as I could, a snap-shot of what they were saying to us about the conditions that they were facing. And then I was drawing my conclusions based on what they were saying and what I was observing, myself. And similarly, having been to Manjaca and Trnopolje, again, I was trying to capture as faithfully as I could what the Serbs were telling us at Manjaca and Prijedor. And, again, it wasn't a verbatim transcript of the meetings, but it was my best effort. And then, again, adding my comments based on my understanding of what I was actually seeing, as well as what I was being told. I think - I would hope - that it's fairly clear that I was being as accurate as I could about how I was reflecting what the Serbs who were talking to me were describing events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If I understood your evidence correctly, you've told us that a person who is in uniform carrying a weapon and involved in combat can be detained as a prisoner of war. Do we understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. That would be -- that would be a shorthand way of describing a -- a typical way of identifying a combatant.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. What would your view be, if you have one, on a person in civilian clothes who's armed and participating in combat? Can that person be legitimately detained?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Depending on -- on -- on what they're doing and where they are, then they're either a combatant or they're a criminal. And, again, you'll be aware of my experience in the army, working in Northern Ireland where there were a group of people wearing civilian clothes and carrying weapons and the British government was very careful to treat them as criminals as opposed to combatants. So I'm aware that you can dance on pinheads around the issue, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. And you would agree with me that in the theatre in Bosnia at the time, where you were, there were both uniformed and non-uniformed groups involved in combat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I didn't actually see people who were not in uniform carrying weapons and in combat. So I saw lots of people wearing lots of different type of uniform belonging to different organisations and units. I didn't actually see people wearing civilian ... well, the one example that I can think of off the top of my head of somebody who was wearing civilian clothes and armed was a gentleman who'd come from the Ministry of Health in Pale when we visited Manjaca, but that's -- he was possibly an exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Referring back to Exhibit P1599, sir, that's the CSCE mission report for 24 August to 4 September 1992, the one we've been looking at. You did not author that report, if I understood it correctly?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And on page 8 of that report we've shown you, at the last paragraph on page 8, where there is mention of uniformed and non-uniformed groups, individuals mobilized directly from their homes, fighting in civilian clothes. Would you have any reason to doubt that information in there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: No. And, again, it's worth noting that the report was written describing the findings of the rapporteur mission across the whole area, and they may well actually have seen more evidence than -- they may have seen evidence of that, where I didn't. In different places.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Would you accept that the people that you saw in detention when you visited the centres, the camps, in civilian clothes may very well have been non-uniformed fighters who were in detention?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: So, in Manjaca they may have been. And, again, the very clear explanation that we've given for Trnopolje was that these were not soldiers, because they were people who were being kept there for their own protection; as opposed to being prisoner of war who were being held there because they were prisoners of war. So it may well have been the case in Manjaca, but I don't think it was the case in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: When you visited Manjaca, did you have the authority to attempt to establish whether or not these people were involved in combat?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether I needed authority to establish that. I wasn't -- I was -- I was talking to them. I'm not quite sure what your question is after, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I will be more specific. Did you discuss with the -- those in charge of detention, those in charge of facility, did you discuss with them why the people were there or seek records showing why the people were detained there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I think that my testimony probably already describes the long explanation that we were given by the gentleman who was running the camp as to how he was running it and why he was running it. And I'm fairly sure that we've probably also, in a separate Trial Chamber, rehearsed the questions that John Thomson asked him. At this stage, I can't -- without looking back at the documentation, I can't actually remember how -- how the conversation went.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, could I just follow up on your last answer to -- to counsel. Because I guess that counsel's question to you was really whether you were told that the detainees at Manjaca were, in fact, POWs. Do you recall whether you were given such information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And -- and I could refer back to my report, if that would help. But we were given a very long explanation of how the Geneva Conventions were being applied to these individuals who were there as prisoner of war. And that explanation was provided by the camp commandant. So as far as he was concerned, he was holding prisoners of war, and he was at pains to explain to us how he was applying the Geneva Conventions correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And were you given at that occasion or at any later occasion any evidence to sustain or to support the characterisation of the detainees as POWs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. So -- so it -- and, again, I would appreciate that people would find it quite hard to be able to show us a chain of evidence that we captured somebody at this point and at that time he was armed and involved in this conflict and then to show us an evidence chain all the way through to an individual actually in Manjaca. So I appreciate it would be difficult to do that, but nobody actually did that. They simply said, These are men who are prisoner of war whom we have captured and are now detaining. And that explanation didn't accord with the explanation that I was given by the people with whom I spoke in Manjaca. And, again, I appreciate that they may have been just making it all up, but that not the impression that I formed at the time. It was very intense little conversations which dried up as soon as somebody got close enough to be able to listen to what was going on, at which point they didn't want to talk about anything. And the impression that I formed was not -- was that these -- these looks like civilians. Again, I don't know, and it's interesting that nobody has raised it, the extent to which all of these people probably carried out military service as conscripts in the JNA at some point before the conflict, and so I have no doubt that many of them at some point would have been trained to use weapons. Many of them may well have been using weapons to defend their homes. But the net product was pretty clear as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you given any information about the armed units to which the detainees were supposed to have belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did the commander provide you with any information about who exactly the enemy was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would understand, My Lord, that he was suggesting that these people had been fighting against the regular Serb forces as the Serb forces tried to protect the Serb population of, for example, Prijedor, from the uprising being carried out by these people against them. That was the -- that was the logic that was being explained. And that didn't quite tie up with the version of events which other people were describing in which the Serb forces, regular or otherwise, were coming to people's house; taking them out; inviting the women and children to move in one direction, the men to move in another direction; incarcerating the men in one set of camps and women and children in another set camps; and then bit by bit allowing them to move into Croatia. And I was involved, as you are aware, in monitoring the release by the ICRC of detainees from both Manjaca and Trnopolje which carried on over time the rest of that year and possibly into January. I can't remember exactly when Manjaca was closed down eventually, but it was a while later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So in your recollection the camp commander depicted the detainees as being members of an armed uprising. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, would it be better, given that Mr. McLeod's pointed out it's been 18 years, if we had his report on the screen, which is part of the package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let me hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My Lord, I can't -- I can't remember whether it was the commandant of Manjaca or the mayor or others we were talking to in Prijedor who were characterising them exactly like that, but certainly between those series of conversation which took place over the couple of days, that was the -- that was the -- that was how they were trying to portray what had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Back to you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we have up, please, on the screen a document which is part of the 92 ter package, which is 10217.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which you've dealt with in your Brdjanin testimony, Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we have a tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. It's tab 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we look at the bottom of the first page of your report, which you've noted down also in your personal notes from which this report was taken: "Colonel Popovic. Welcome to this PW camp. My name is Colonel ... Popovic. I am the commandant of this camp. I want to stress this is a PW camp and not a concentration camp." And then started to refer to the Geneva Conventions. And as I think you pointed out, he appeared to have a prepared script. Is that right Mr. McLeod?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "There are around 3.640 prisoners of war in this camp." And then he goes back to the Geneva Convention articles. "The people in the camp have been caught in the zone of combat in accord with Article 4 of the Geneva Conventions, numbers 1, 2," et cetera, et cetera. Which specify who can be a prisoner of war. And then I think he went through what he was doing to comply, as he put it, with the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Paragraph 21: "You are probably interested in the nationality of the prisoner of war." There are 125 Croats, 3.4 per cent; Serbs 0.04; and Muslims, 96.5. And then there was a specific inquiry about a particular Canadian Croat, I think. Can we go to the next page, and this may deal with what Judge Harhoff was asking you about. Paragraph 33. Just above paragraph 33, the commandant was asked how the prisoners of war were actually taken, if they were actually fighting or carrying weapons." And the response: "There is an interrogation period. Everyone is being interrogated. And if it is proven that he did not take part in the fighting, he will be free." Now the question, I don't know whether presumably but one of the members of the commission rather than you, Mr. McLeod, was a direct one: How were they taken? Was that the only answer that he gave?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: That appears to the only answer that I wrote down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: And then wrote up in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And were you making notes at the time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yep. And I think -- and perhaps we'd just better look at the last page of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm terribly sorry, but I note that there might be a -- a wrong translation of this document. Because that might make a confusion. It's -- paragraph 33, can we have it back? Paragraph 33 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... sorry, it's an English report. I'm reading from the English -- I don't know -- I'm sorry. I'm reading -- this is an English report written in English. I don't know how it's been translated; I can't help that. But if you say there's a mistake, Mr. Zecevic, then we can correct it. But We're not going --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry, I mixed it up, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we go back to the last page, please. I agree it's unusual to have a report in English translated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there we get, as I already put to you, paragraph 36: "The general impression. Colonel Popovic was speaking from a prepared script, quoted the Geneva Conventions by rote, ... he was very sensitive on the subject what he did with prisoners who stepped out of line, refusing to give any more explanation than ... they were dealt with in accordance with the Geneva Conventions." Just two other matters that arise from what you were asked, by Mr. Krgovic largely. Can I just go back to the part ... this was at page 46. Mr. Krgovic asked you a question about -- that the: "... that the war waged ... was far from an" [sic] "organised combat between uniformed armies serving recognised governments and honouring the rules of war. Isn't that correct?" And you said: "No. I think it was quite clear, and not just in northern Bosnia but in each of the various areas where I worked, that there were political and military structures in place." I just want to clarify so that the Chamber understands your experience, Mr. McLeod: For how long were you a monitor based in the former Yugoslavia for ECMM?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: So I spent a year with ECMM. I spent the following year working for the international conference working for Thorvald Stoltenberg's deputies as a political advisor. So I was there for two years in total.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you just give, again, the Trial Chamber a rough area - a rough area -- a rough idea of which -- which areas you worked?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: So with ECMM I worked out of Zagreb, so in Croatia looking at the -- the -- the issues between the Croatian government and the Krajina Serbs, so in the UNPAs. I went into northern Bosnia, and so -- met the Serbs in northern Bosnian and went to Manjaca and Trnopolje. And I also worked in Central Bosnia and so saw what was happening between the Croats and the Muslims in the Vitez-Zenica area. And the second year was negotiations between the Croatian government and the Krajina Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Last topic. You were shown this document which was dated the 21st of August. Perhaps we better have it up again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, 607. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This purports to be a directive emanating from Mr. Zupljanin dated the 21st of August and referring back to an order issued by the Ministry of the Interior about giving protection to people who were then going to be released from these camps. You had a visit the day before when Mr. Zupljanin was present to Banja Luka. Did he -- if he had mentioned to you that he was -- had issued such an order in respect of people who were going to be released, would that be something that you would have recorded?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you went back on the 24th of August when Mr. Bulic was present for a short time. If he had said to you, We, the police, are going to be protecting anybody who's being released, is that something you would have recorded?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Again, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McLeod. Just one last question. Do you recall whether the ECMM had made any determination as to the nature of the armed conflicts at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. So there was clearly armed conflict going on between the armies of Croatia and Bosanska Krajina, if you like. And -- and that -- that -- that was quite clearly going on, and that carried on intermittently for the next 18 months or so. And there was an ethnic cleansing going on, and ethnic cleansing was taking place particularly from northern Bosnia expelling Muslims and from Croatia expelling Serbs. And to an extent it was also taking place, but to a far less extent, from the -- the -- the Bosnian-controlled areas in Central Bosnia and Bihac and so on. And ethnic cleansing was not an armed conflict; it was a one-way -- fundamentally, a one-way street on -- being carried out by -- by particularly two of the parties and, to a limited extent, by the third party as well. So I would -- clearly there was -- there was a -- a fairly conventional war going on between different parties, and all of them ended up fighting each other at different points in Bosnia. And that had characteristics which were pretty clear. And you could talk to the military commanders and invite them to stop and then organise a cease-fire and then invite them to withdraw their troops and weaponry and so on, and I was engaged in -- in inspecting Croatian tanks, for example, that had been withdrawn from the contact line in Croatia to find out where they were, and I wrote down the -- the numbers of the tanks, which was quite amusing. So -- so that type of warfare was going on, and then there was ethnic cleansing, which was completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you're saying that the armed conflict that took part between the Croatian forces and the Serb forces was an international armed conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Between -- well, at the time, to call it an international armed conflict would have been a -- quite a difficult thing to do from some government's point of view, because they didn't want to recognise some of the people who were taking part in the armed conflict as nations. And so the people in Bosanska Krajina would have argued very strongly that they were a nation, and so their conflict with Croatia was an international conflict. The people within the -- the -- the -- and, again, Bosanska Krajina, which stretched into Croatia, as one party, would define it, but not in terms of another party defining it. So, again, the conflict between the Serbs and the Croats within Croatia between the UNPA and the Croatian-controlled parts of Croatia: From one party's point of view that was an international conflict, and from the other party's point of view it was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: But regular forces fighting each other as you would recognise regular forces fighting each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Which brings me back to my original question: Did the ECMM make any determination of the conflicts in terms of whether it was international or internal at the time you were there, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Um ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... sorry. The alternative would be that the ECMM simply left the question open. So I'm interested to know whether actually any determination was made with the ECMM as to what kind of international -- armed conflict was going on.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly, Your Honour. So ECMM was acutely aware of the fact that there was -- of the recognition issue. And as I've described, I think, even in testimony here, if not in the previous Trial Chamber, we had to very careful not to provide recognition of Bosanska Krajina as a -- as a nation, because it hadn't been recognised by -- by governments. And, therefore, yes, ECMM was acutely aware of the issue of providing recognition of nationhood, when the member governments hadn't actually recognised any of the factions who were claiming nation status as nations. So, yes, we were pretty aware of whether this was an international conflict or internal conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: How are we to interpret your answer?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: So as far as the fighting that was taking place within northern Bosnia was concerned, that was not an international conflict. The fighting that was taking place between the Serbs in northern Bosnia and the Croats on the other side of the river in Croatia, that would be an international conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I just -- I think there are two matters that need to be clarified arising from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, you've said in your answer to Judge Harhoff: "... ethnic cleansing was not an armed conflict; it was a one-way -- fundamentally, a one-way street ... being carried out by particularly two of the parties and, to a limited extent, by the third ..." Who do you mean by the first two, and who -- and which was the third?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought I -- I thought I mentioned that in my answer. So, the Serbs and the Croats went in for fairly extensive ethnic cleansing, and I -- I saw, I went and had a look in Central Bosnia to see, to a more limited extent, the Bosnian, as well, had cleared a Croatian village, for example. So each of the parties did it. But by far the greatest amount was carried out by the Serbs and then the Croats and then the Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, you mentioned the Bosanska Krajina government. Just to be clear, are you referring there to the -- which hadn't obtained recognition, are you referring there to the government headed by Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... or to a ore localised one?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: No. The -- the -- so the Serb Republic was the -- was the overarching state, with its headquarters in Pale. And then a -- Bosanska Krajina - and, again, I'm not the expert, but my friends here would know it inside out - was the -- I would understand the region of northern Bosnia which would then stretch also into Croatia, controlled by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So your talk -- I see what you mean. You're actually talking about what's come to be known as the RSK, the part in Croatia between Croatia and the border; is that right? Because there are two Krajinas.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: The -- the -- I've actually talked about both, just to be confusing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The -- okay. The two Krajinas is what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES GEORGE ALEXANDER McLEOD
utterances.text: In different answers I referred to both of them, and we'd have to go back and unpick the answers. If -- My Lords, if you're not clear, then please come back and quiz me one more time so that you can be clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Sorry, Your Honour, I just thought we'd better clarify the first bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I believe your application is still alive, but for continuity, can you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, can I move into evidence the whole 92 ter package, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the 92 ter package will be given the prefix of Exhibit 1727. The internal memo regarding the subsequent documents of the package will be filed subsequently. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm -- please correct me if I'm wrong, Ms. Korner, but there was a portion of this package that was to have been separately placed under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, Your Honour, any of the documents -- would it be simpler if we simply identify to the Registry the documents which need to be under seal? It's effectively all the reports, bar the CSCE one, need to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Again, whatever works. If the Registry ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll identify that to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. McLeod, we thank you for your assistance to the Tribunal once more, and you are now released as a witness. We wish you a safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we take the adjournment for the day, there are a number of matters which were raised by the Prosecution at the beginning of today's sitting to which the Trial Chamber would wish to speak. The first is -- and my recollection is that counsel for the Prosecution, Ms. Korner, had suggested that a date be fixed for a 65 ter meeting. In the view of the Chamber, the more efficient way of dealing with the several outstanding issues which would have been canvassed at such a meeting would be to conduct a Status Conference, and such a conference will be held during the week, having regard to the schedule of witnesses as intimated by Ms. Korner, the week beginning the 6th of December. That is according to the convenience of the progress of witnesses. And the parties at that time should be prepared to discuss the scheduling of the remainder of the case. The second matter deals with Witness 228. The Chamber does not see a need to postpone hearing Witness 228, given the likelihood that the situation which the OTP alluded to may occur, that is, that there may not be witnesses to call during the last week before the recess. Furthermore, it is impossible at this moment to predict exactly when this witness will be testifying in the Karadzic case. The Trial Chamber is, therefore, hesitant to rely on the possibility of having this witness testify in this case while here to testify in Karadzic. If the witness is unfit to travel, then the Office of the Prosecution may, of course, move to hear the witness via videolink. The third matter is the commencement of proceedings after the winter recess. And having heard the representations of counsel for the Defence, the Chamber reiterates that proceedings will resume on 10th of January, 2011. But the Chamber requests the Registry to organise an extra session on that day, that is, Monday the 10th. On the 11th of January, the case will be as scheduled. But on the 12th of January, the Wednesday, the hearing will resume at 3.00 in the afternoon. Thereafter, the case will be adjourned for the Thursday and Friday and, depending on the progress of the Prosecution's case, would resume on Monday, the 17th of January. The final issue is Witness 223 being heard during Witness 224's videolink. The Chamber has considered the application made in relation to ST-223, who is reported to be unwell and unable to travel to The Hague to testify on the date proposed by the Prosecution. Taking into account the requirement under the Statute to ensure that the proceedings are fair and expeditious and also for reasons of judicial economy, the Chamber is satisfied, in the exceptional circumstances of 223, that it would be in the interests of justice to permit the witness to testify over the previously-ordered video-conference link to be established from 223's country of residence for the preceding witness, 224. This is provided that the necessary arrangements can be made in time by the Registry. So we take the adjournment to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I just ask about the Mladic notebook witnesses. I mean, that was one of the -- and it is, in a sense, one of the more urgent. Because if they are to come, to be dealt with, then one of them certainly needs to be seen in his own country next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In terms of the work that the Chamber has set out for itself to do for the remainder of the day, that is one of the items, and we trust that we would be able to rule on that tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of November, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
